summary: Defines EAP-NOOB, an authentication method for setting up Internet-of-Things devices that ship with no pre-installed credentials. The device and server exchange keys over the network, and a short message carried out-of-band, such as a displayed code or a blinking light, lets the user confirm the exchange was not tampered with. The device needs some non-network way to show or receive that message. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: EAP-NOOB is a way to let a device with no password join a network. The device and the network server swap keys over the network, and the user carries a short message between them, out of band, to prove that nobody tampered with the swap.

questions: how to onboard iot devices without credentials
how does out of band authentication work in eap
what is the eap-noob oob step
subtitle: How a gadget with no credentials joins a network: swap keys over the air, then confirm them with a one-way message a person carries.

tldr.problem: A device bought off the shelf has no identifier and no password, and often has only a light or a speaker to talk to the user.
tldr.mechanism: The device and the server agree a key over the network, then a short message carried by the user out of band confirms that the key exchange was not tampered with.
tldr.outcome: The device gets its own secret key, different for every device, without a pre-printed password. RFC 9140 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 9965.

today: RFC 9140 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2021. It was later updated by RFC 9965, which covers the eap.arpa. domain the method relies on, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Devices Need Another Way In
sections.content:
The document describes a method for registration, authentication and key derivation for network-connected smart devices, such as consumer and enterprise appliances in the Internet of Things. These devices may be off-the-shelf hardware sold and distributed without any prior registration or credential-provisioning process, or they may be recycled devices after a hard reset. The device registration in a server database, the ownership of the device, and the authentication credentials for both network access and application-level security must all be established at the time the device is deployed. Many such devices have only limited user interfaces, often limited to either only input, such as a camera, or only output, such as a display screen. The task is made harder by the fact that the devices may exist in large numbers and may have to be deployed or reconfigured quickly as user needs change.

Summarised, the devices may have no pre-established relation with the intended server or user, no pre-provisioned device identifier or authentication credentials, or an input or output interface capable only of one-directional out-of-band communication.

Many proprietary out-of-band configuration methods exist for specific devices. The goal of the specification is to provide an open standard and a generic protocol for bootstrapping the security of network-connected appliances such as displays, printers, speakers and cameras. The security bootstrapping uses a user-assisted out-of-band channel. The device authentication relies on a user having physical access to the device, and the key exchange security is based on the assumption that attackers cannot observe or modify the messages conveyed through that channel. The approach is the one taken in pairing protocols: perform a Diffie-Hellman key exchange over the insecure network and authenticate the established key with the help of the out-of-band channel, to prevent impersonation attacks.

The solution is intended for devices that have a non-network input or output interface, such as a camera, microphone, display screen, speaker or blinking LED, able to send or receive dynamically generated messages of tens of bytes. It may not be appropriate for very small sensors or actuators with no user interface at all, or for devices the user cannot reach. The out-of-band channel is assumed to be at least partly automated, for example a camera scanning a bar code, so there is no need to minimise the length of the data transferred, unlike Bluetooth pairing where it is essential to keep the manually transferred code short. The out-of-band messages are dynamically generated, so static printed registration codes are not supported. One reason for requiring dynamic messages is that the receipt of the message authorises the server to take ownership of the device, and dynamic messages are more secure than printed codes, which could be leaked and later misused.
sections.plainLanguage: Many small devices are sold with nothing pre-loaded, and the person setting them up may only be able to see a blinking light or hear a tone. This document gives those devices a standard way to join a network safely, using a short message the person carries from the device to the network.

sections.title: The Association State Machine
sections.content:
One EAP-NOOB method execution spans two or more EAP conversations, called exchanges here. Each exchange consists of several EAP request-response pairs. At least two separate EAP conversations are needed, to give the human user time to deliver the out-of-band message between them.

The protocol starts with the Initial Exchange, which comprises four EAP request-response pairs. The server allocates an identifier to the peer, and the two negotiate the protocol version and the cryptosuite, that is the cryptographic algorithm suite, exchange nonces, and perform an Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The user-assisted out-of-band step then takes place, and it needs only one out-of-band message, either from the peer to the server or from the server to the peer. While waiting for that step, the peer MAY probe the server by reconnecting to it with EAP-NOOB. If the step has already taken place, the probe leads to the Completion Exchange, which completes the mutual authentication and the key confirmation. If it has not, the probe leads to the Waiting Exchange, and the peer performs another probe after a server-defined minimum waiting time. The Initial Exchange and the Waiting Exchange always end in EAP-Failure, while the Completion Exchange may result in EAP-Success. Once the peer and the server have performed a successful Completion Exchange, both store the created association in persistent storage, and the out-of-band step is not repeated. New temporal keys, rekeying and updates of the cryptographic algorithms are then handled by the Reconnect Exchange.

The association state machine is the same for the server and the peer, and has five states. The Unregistered state, numbered 0, holds no state information. The Waiting for OOB state, numbered 1, and the OOB Received state, numbered 2, are ephemeral. The Reconnecting state, numbered 3, and the Registered state, numbered 4, are persistent. Before a successful Completion Exchange the state is ephemeral in both ends, and a timeout or error may send one or both back to the Unregistered state so that the Initial Exchange is repeated. Only a user reset or a memory failure can return an endpoint from the persistent states to the ephemeral ones.

The server MUST NOT repeat a successful out-of-band step with the same peer unless the user explicitly resets the association or the server loses the persistent storage. Once the association has entered the Registered state, the server MUST NOT delete it or go back to the ephemeral states without explicit user approval, and the peer MUST NOT repeat the out-of-band step unless the user deletes the association or resets the peer to the Unregistered state.

A special feature of the method is that the server is not assumed to have any prior knowledge of the peer, so the peer initially uses the generic identity string noob@eap-noob.arpa as its Network Access Identifier. The server then allocates a server-specific identifier to the peer. The generic identifier serves two purposes: it tells the server that the peer supports and expects the EAP-NOOB method, and it allows the routing of EAP-NOOB sessions to a specific authentication server in an AAA architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends keep the same five-step state: not registered, waiting for the message, message received, reconnecting, and registered. The message the user carries moves them from waiting to received, and a final exchange confirms the keys and moves them to registered.

sections.title: The Exchanges
sections.content:
All EAP-NOOB exchanges start with a common handshake. It begins with the identity request and response common to all EAP methods, whose purpose is to let the AAA architecture route the conversation to the right server and let the server select the EAP method. The handshake continues with one EAP-NOOB request-response pair in which the server discovers the peer identifier and the peer state. The server then chooses which exchange follows, based on the combination of the peer and server states. If either is Unregistered and the other is in one of the ephemeral states, the Initial Exchange is chosen. If either is in the OOB Received state and the other is in the Waiting for OOB or OOB Received state, the out-of-band step has taken place and the Completion Exchange is chosen. If both are in the Waiting for OOB state, the Waiting Exchange is chosen. If the peer is in the Reconnecting state and the server is in the Registered or Reconnecting state, the Reconnect Exchange is chosen. All other combinations are error situations where user action is required, and the server SHOULD indicate them with error code 2002.

The Initial Exchange adds two further request-response pairs to the handshake. In the first, type 2, the server sends a newly allocated peer identifier, an optional new Network Access Identifier, the list of protocol versions and cryptosuites it supports, an indicator of the out-of-band channel directions it supports, and a ServerInfo object. The peer replies with the version and cryptosuite it picked, the received identifier, the channel direction it picked, and a PeerInfo object. In the second pair, type 3, the two exchange the public components of their ECDHE keys and their nonces. The Initial Exchange always ends with EAP-Failure, because authentication cannot yet be completed. Both ends then move to the Waiting for OOB state.

The OOB Step carries three data fields: the peer identifier, a secret nonce called Noob, and a cryptographic fingerprint called Hoob. The receiver compares the received fingerprint with a value it computed locally, which is an integrity check that ensures the two ends agree on the contents of the Initial Exchange. If the values match, the receiver moves to the OOB Received state; otherwise it MUST reject the message, and it SHOULD tell the user whether the message was accepted or rejected. A receiver SHOULD reject invalid messages without changing its state until an application-specific number of invalid messages, OobRetries, has been reached, and then go back to the Unregistered state.

The sender may send several out-of-band messages with different Noob values while waiting. The Noob values expire after an application-dependent timeout, and the server MUST NOT accept Noob values older than that in the Completion Exchange. The recommended value for that timeout is 3600 seconds. The sender typically generates a new Noob at constant intervals, with the recommended interval being half the timeout, so the receiver will accept either of the two latest values.

The Completion Exchange has one or two further request-response pairs. If the peer is waiting for the out-of-band message, only the type 6 pair takes place, and the server sends the NoobId value that identifies the exact message the server received. If the peer has already received the message, the direction was server to peer, and a type 5 pair comes first so that the server can learn the NoobId the peer holds; the server then returns the same value in the type 6 pair. In that final pair the two exchange message authentication codes. Both sides MUST compare the received code with a locally computed value, and the exchange ends in EAP-Success only if the peer finds the correct MACs and the server finds the correct MACp. Otherwise the failing endpoint reports error code 4001 and the exchange ends in EAP-Failure. After a successful Completion Exchange both ends move to the Registered state, derive the output keying material and store the persistent association.

The Waiting Exchange has one further request-response pair and always ends in EAP-Failure. It tells the peer that the server has not yet received the out-of-band message. The server may send a minimum time to wait before probing again, and the peer waits at least that long, or an application-specified default if the server sent nothing.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange runs in four parts: the server and the device agree a key, the person carries a short message between them, the two use that message to prove the key exchange was genuine, and the server finally confirms the session. The device can check back partway through, and the server tells it to wait.

sections.title: The Messages and Their Fields
sections.content:
The in-band messages are JSON objects in UTF-8 encoding. The important fields are these.

  • PeerId is the peer identifier allocated by the server in the Initial Exchange. It must follow the syntax of the utf8-username of RFC 7542, and the server must generate it so it does not repeat and cannot be guessed before it is sent. One way is a random 16-byte identifier, base64url encoded without padding into a 22-character ASCII string. The peer copies it byte by byte from the message where it was allocated, and the server compares the received and the previously allocated identifier byte by byte.
  • NAI and NewNAI are the peer's Network Access Identifier and a new one the server may assign. The default is noob@eap-noob.arpa, and the peer may be configured with another. The server-assigned identifier allows more flexible routing of the EAP sessions over the AAA infrastructure, including roaming, and some authenticators use its realm part to pick connection parameters for that peer.
  • Type is the message type, an integer from 0 to 9, and requests and their responses share the same value.
  • PeerState is an integer from 0 to 4, although only 0 to 3 are ever sent.
  • PKs and PKp are the public components of the ECDHE keys, sent in the JSON Web Key format.
  • Cryptosuites and Cryptosuitep are the identifiers of the suites the server supports and the one the peer chose. The server must send a non-empty array with no repeating elements, ordered by decreasing priority, and the peer must respond with exactly one suite.
  • Dirs and Dirp indicate the out-of-band channel directions the server supports and the peer selected, with 1 for peer-to-server, 2 for server-to-peer and 3 for both.
  • Ns and Np are the 32-byte nonces of the Initial Exchange, and the secret nonce Noob is 16 bytes. All the nonces are fresh random byte strings generated by the endpoint that sends them.
  • ServerInfo and PeerInfo are JSON objects of at most 500 bytes each, carrying information from the EAP method to the application layer, such as the access network name or the peer brand, model and serial number, which help the user deliver the out-of-band message to the right place.
  • SleepTime is the number of seconds the peer must not start a new execution of the method with the authenticator, unless it receives the out-of-band message or the user acts. It is an unsigned integer from 0 to 3600.
  • Noob is the 16-byte secret nonce sent through the out-of-band channel and used for the session key derivation.
  • Hoob is the 16-byte cryptographic fingerprint computed from all the parameters exchanged in the Initial Exchange and in the out-of-band message. Receiving it over the out-of-band channel guarantees the integrity of the key exchange and the parameter negotiation.
  • NoobId is a 16-byte identifier for the out-of-band message, computed with a one-way function from the Noob value.
  • MACs and MACp are the message authentication codes used for mutual authentication, key confirmation and integrity checking.

The fingerprint and the identifier are computed with the hash function of the negotiated cryptosuite, truncated to the 16 leftmost bytes of the output, and the message authentication codes are computed with HMAC and truncated to the 32 leftmost bytes. The inputs are JSON arrays of a fixed 17 elements, copied verbatim from the sent and received messages, with no reordering and no added white space. The nonces and the hash value must be base64url encoded when used as input to the cryptographic functions and when sent as JSON strings, and all base64url encoding is done without padding. In the key derivation, the unencoded bytes are used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is a small JSON object. The parts that matter are the identifier the server gives the device, the secret and the fingerprint that travel with the person, and the authentication codes that prove both ends hold the same keys.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Authentication
sections.content:
EAP-NOOB derives the EAP output values MSK and EMSK and other secret keying material from the output of an Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman algorithm, using a two-ephemeral-key and no-static-key scheme. In the Initial Exchange and the Reconnect Exchange the two compute the ECDHE shared secret Z. In the Completion Exchange and the Reconnect Exchange they compute the secret keying material from Z with a one-step key derivation function, whose auxiliary hash function comes from the negotiated cryptosuite.

There are four keying modes. Mode 0 is the Completion Exchange, always with ECDHE. Mode 1 is a Reconnect Exchange that rekeys without ECDHE. Mode 2 is a Reconnect Exchange that rekeys with ECDHE and no change of cryptosuite. Mode 3 is a Reconnect Exchange that rekeys with ECDHE and a newly negotiated cryptosuite.

In the Completion Exchange the input Z comes from the preceding Initial Exchange, and the key derivation function also takes the AlgorithmId, which is the fixed 8-byte ASCII string "EAP-NOOB", the two nonces, and the secret Noob from the out-of-band message. In the simplest Reconnect Exchange, mode 1, fresh nonces are exchanged but no ECDHE keys are sent, and the input Z is replaced with the shared key Kz from the persistent association. That gives rekeying without the cost of the ECDHE exchange, but also without forward secrecy. When forward secrecy is wanted, in modes 2 and 3, both nonces and ECDHE keys are exchanged, the input Z is the fresh shared secret, and the inputs also include the shared key Kz from the persistent association, which binds the rekeying output to the previously authenticated keys.

The output bytes are used for the MSK, the EMSK, an Application Main Session Key that may be used for application-layer security, a method identifier, and the message authentication keys. The Completion Exchange produces the shared secret Kz, which the two store in the persistent association.

The mutual authentication rests on two features, both carried in the out-of-band message. The first is the secret nonce Noob, which the two use in the Completion Exchange to mutually authenticate the session key created with ECDHE; on its own, the message authentication codes computed with Noob are enough to authenticate the key exchange. The second is the integrity-protecting fingerprint Hoob, whose purpose is to stop impersonation attacks even in situations where an attacker can eavesdrop on the out-of-band channel and the Noob value is compromised. On some human-assisted channels, such as human-perceptible audio or a user-typed URL, it may be easier to notice tampering than to notice disclosure of the message, and those applications benefit from the fingerprint.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared key comes from an elliptic-curve key exchange, and the secret from the out-of-band message is mixed into it. Two separate things travel with the user: a secret that proves both ends hold the same key, and a fingerprint that reveals any tampering with the exchange.

sections.title: Registered Values
sections.content:
The EAP method type for EAP-NOOB, value 56, has been assigned in the Method Types subregistry of the EAP registry. A new registry called "Nimble Out-of-Band Authentication for EAP Parameters (EAP-NOOB)" has been created, with subregistries for cryptosuites, message types, error codes and the ServerInfo and PeerInfo data fields.

Each cryptosuite specifies an ECDHE curve for the key exchange, the encoding of the ECDHE public key as a JSON Web Key object, and a cryptographic hash function for the fingerprint, the HMAC computation and the key derivation. The hash output must be at least 32 bytes. The initial values are 1, which uses the Curve25519 curve, the JSON Web Key public-key format and SHA-256, with the JWK encoding using a crv of X25519 and a kty of OKP, and 2, which uses the NIST P-256 curve, the JSON Web Key public-key format and SHA-256, with a crv of P-256 and a kty of EC. Implementations MUST support cryptosuite 1, and support for cryptosuite 2 is RECOMMENDED. New values are assigned through IANA with the Specification Required policy.

The message types are 0 for an error notification, 1 for the peer identifier and state discovery used in all exchanges, 2 for version, cryptosuite and parameter negotiation in the Initial Exchange, 3 for the exchange of ECDHE keys and nonces in the Initial Exchange, 4 for the indication in the Waiting Exchange that the server has not yet received an out-of-band message, 5 for NoobId discovery in the Completion Exchange, 6 for authentication and key confirmation with HMAC in the Completion Exchange, 7 for negotiation in the Reconnect Exchange, 8 for the exchange of ECDHE keys and nonces in the Reconnect Exchange, and 9 for authentication and key confirmation with HMAC in the Reconnect Exchange.

The error codes are 1001 for an invalid Network Access Identifier, 1002 for an invalid message structure, 1003 for invalid data, 1004 for an unexpected message type, 1005 for an invalid ECDHE key, 2001 for an unwanted peer, 2002 for a state mismatch needing user action, 2003 for an unrecognised out-of-band message identifier, 2004 for an unexpected peer identifier, 3001 for no mutually supported protocol version, 3002 for no mutually supported cryptosuite, 3003 for no mutually supported out-of-band direction, 4001 for an HMAC verification failure, 5001 for an application-specific error, 5002 for invalid server information, 5003 for an invalid server URL, 5004 for invalid peer information, and 6001 to 6999 reserved for private and experimental use.

The special-use domain name eap-noob.arpa has been registered in the .arpa registry and in the Special-Use Domain Names registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers the numbers the protocol uses: the EAP method number, the two cryptographic suites that may be chosen, the ten message types, and the error codes. It also reserves the domain name used by the default identity.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EAP-NOOB is an authentication and key derivation protocol, so security considerations appear in most sections of the specification. The design rests on an authenticated ECDHE key exchange and on the assumption that the out-of-band channel cannot be observed or modified by an attacker.

The reliance on the user to identify the correct device is an inherent property of user-assisted out-of-band authentication. If the user mistakenly delivers the message from the wrong device to the server, the server may create an association with the wrong peer. An attacker who substitutes a compromised device is in effect mounting a supply chain attack, where the user accepts a compromised physical device. EAP-NOOB is not vulnerable to an opportunistic attacker who plays an audio or blinking light message to a device that is not expecting it, because the out-of-band message has no value to anyone who did not take part in the corresponding Initial Exchange.

Certification of peer devices can mitigate user mistakes, because a certificate or an attestation token can convey authentic identifiers and attributes such as the model and serial number. Compared with a fully certificate-based authentication, EAP-NOOB needs no trusted third party and does not require the user to know any identifier of the device; physical access is enough. A dedicated app on a mobile device that talks to a server at a preconfigured URL protects against the attacker tricking the user into delivering the message to the wrong server.

After registration, an attacker could clone the device identity by copying the keys from the persistent association into another device. That threat is mitigated by creating the keys and storing the association in a secure hardware component such as a trusted execution environment, and by remote attestation at the application level. A Reconnect Exchange with a new cryptosuite also disconnects all but the first clone that performs the update.

A trusted path is needed between the user and the device, because a spoofed user interface on a device could otherwise make a registered device under an attacker's control behave like an unregistered one. Such a path can be implemented by having the user press a reset button to return the device to the Unregistered state and to invoke a trusted interface, but the problem is that these paths are not standardised across devices. A spoofed interface also enables the misbinding attack, where a compromised device tricks the user into registering a different, uncompromised device.

Forward secrecy during fast reconnect is optional: the Reconnect Exchange provides it only if both ends send fresh ECDHE keys. The server MUST NOT reuse the same ECDHE key with the same peer when rekeying with ECDHE, but may simply not send an ECDHE key at all, which is KeyingMode 1. The users delivering the out-of-band messages will often authenticate themselves to the EAP server, for example by logging into a secure web page, which lets the server associate the peer device with the user account.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole scheme rests on the person carrying the message being able to tell the right device from the wrong one, and on the assumption that nobody else can see or change what they carry. The document also covers cloning, spoofed screens and fake servers.

items.text: The identifier the server allocates to the device, typically 22 ASCII characters, and it must be unguessable.

items.text: The 16-byte secret nonce that travels with the user and is mixed into the session key.

items.text: The 16-byte fingerprint of the whole exchange, so the receiver can detect tampering.

items.text: A 16-byte identifier derived from Noob, so each end names the same message.

items.text: The 32-byte nonces of the Initial Exchange, and Ns2 and Np2 for the Reconnect Exchange.

items.title: MACs and MACp
items.text: The message authentication codes that confirm both ends hold the same key.
